subject: unicornFoal
pitch: A newborn unicorn foal on wobbly long legs. A pearly white coat with a soft lilac shimmer, a short fluffy mane and tail in pastel pink, mint and lavender, a small spiralled horn in gold, big dark eyes with long lashes, little silver hooves, and a daisy chain hanging around its neck.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the newborn unicorn foal model as a single TypeScript module using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, focusing on API calls I'm confident are correct since I won't be able to test it. I'm thinking through realistic proportions for a newborn foal at real-world scale before writing the code.

Sketching the skeleton joint coordinates...

Still defining joint structure...

I'll go with explicit hips as root joint, then attach the spine chain to it, matching the reference pattern. Now I'm planning the neck chain running from chest up to head, and starting to think through the torso tube sweep radii along the spine.

Working out the actual proportions: body center around y 0.64-0.66, with rump/mid/chest radii tapering, legs reaching down to the ground giving the foal its characteristically long-legged newborn look, and the neck/head extending up and forward with a proportionally large head to match a realistic foal silhouette near 0.9-1.0m tall.

Now I'm figuring out the leg geometry using inverse kinematics — setting up shoulder root points and hoof targets, then checking whether the upper leg, forearm, and cannon segment lengths sum to enough distance to reach from shoulder down to the ground without the limb looking overly straight or stiff.

For the fetlock, I'll bend it backward to pair with the forward-bending knee, mimicking that digitigrade-like foal stance.

For the hindleg, I'm thinking through the stifle and hock orientation—stifle bending forward, hock bending back—and mapping out segment lengths across hip, stifle, hock, and fetlock joints.

I'm now settling on using a three-segment limb function for each leg, where the chain returns root, two intermediate joints, and the hoof tip, naming each joint accordingly for both front and hind legs.

For the leg chains, the shoulder/hip joint needs to parent to the correct spine joint—chest for forelegs, hips for hindlegs—and the chain config uses role "leg" with a tip defaulting to the contact point. I'm also noting joint names must match a valid identifier pattern, and now I'm setting up the tapering radius for leg segments, starting around 0.06 at the thigh down to 0.035 at the knee.

Continuing, I'm tapering further to thinner cannon and fetlock radii to get that long, thin newborn-foal leg look, using a smooth radius array sweep across the whole leg chain so the skin follows the joints automatically. For the hooves, I'm thinking of them as a short tapered frustum near the ground at the tip of each leg chain, silver-colored, either as its own geometry piece or a small sweep segment from the pastern down to the floor.

Rather than ending the leg sweep with a rounded cap, I'll shape the hoof as a lathe profile around a vertical axis at the hoof's position, building the outline point-by-point so the bottom sits flat at y=0 and widens slightly before narrowing up into the pastern, giving a believable cup-like hoof shape that meets the ground exactly.

Checking that the legs stay within the body silhouette: shoulder root sits inside the body shape, so legs placed at x=±0.11 look reasonably plump for a foal. I'm figuring out the leg targets—forelegs under the chest around z=0.2, hind hooves roughly under the hock near z=-0.12 to -0.16, with hip joints near the rump at z=-0.24.

Measuring limb distances versus bone-segment sums to make sure the legs bend naturally rather than overextend—both front and hind legs come out slightly bent, giving that gawky, long-legged newborn foal look, which fits. I'll trust the limb-solving API to handle the bend plane using the root, target, and hint direction rather than trying to hand-calculate the angles myself.

Now I'm thinking about how to build the torso: sweeping the spine chain with a radius profile so the body bends along with the spine joints, keeping the shape simple and blocky to match the stylized toy-like aesthetic, maybe using a basic circular cross-section rather than anything more elaborate like a belly bulge.

For the mane and tail I want short, fluffy tufts in pastel pink, mint, and lavender. I'm weighing whether to use textured cards (small greyscale SVG tuft drawings tinted by the part's color) placed along the neck for the mane and at the hip for the tail base, versus simple puff-shaped blobs -- cards seem like the better route since I can control the tint and layer several colors for a playful, multi-toned fluffy look.

I should make the tuft texture white-filled so tinting works correctly, since white multiplied by any paint color just produces that color. Now I'm sketching a simple teardrop-shaped SVG path for the tuft shape with strands, filled solid white.

For the mane, I want to scatter cards along the top ridge of the neck surface, filtering by normal direction so only the upper/dorsal surfaces get cards, letting them flow backward along the neck curve.

For the backward-flowing flow direction, going along -Z moves back toward the withers, roughly tracing the crest from poll down the neck, which fits a mane shape. I'm thinking mane cards sized small with pastel colors cycling through pink, mint, lavender, with some bend and variation using a seeded rng for natural scatter.

For the tail, I'm planning it to extend from the hips backward and slightly upward then curving down, built as a tapered tube chain with a fluffy tuft of cards at the tip pointing outward. I'm working out a four-point path for the tail creating three spans plus a tip joint, then sweeping a tapering radius along that chain for the tail shape.

For the tuft, I need the cards' orientation to follow the tail's outward normal rather than the tangent, so they splay outward like fur instead of sticking straight out as spikes—using the sweep's frame-at function to get the right facing direction for each card.

I'm also considering making the fluffy tail a ring of cards around multiple points along the tail, roughly two dozen frames varying in position and angle, with small widths and short lengths so they read as fuzz rather than blades, rooted slightly inside the surface for a natural sink.

Now I'm thinking through the mane and a forelock tuft near the forehead, then moving to the ears -- small rounded foal ears extruded as thin flat plates, oriented so their width runs forward and their height runs upward, figuring out the thickness direction from the cross product of those two axes so the ear sits naturally against the side of the head.

Working out the ear outline coordinates, with a small sharp tip point and smoothing, keeping the geometry simple and colored in coat tone, possibly with a pink inner paint detail. I'm weighing construction methods: either sprouting a coiled spiral shape from the skull hit point with tapering radius and point-capped end, or building it as a straight spiral that winds around its own axis with defined turns, radius, and pitch.

Working out the turn count and pitch so the horn's total length along its axis matches roughly 0.11-0.12 units, with 2.5 turns giving smooth tube knots every quarter turn. For the head I'm planning the muzzle and nose as soft pink features appropriate for a newborn, and thinking through whether to build the skull and jaw as a sweep or lathe shape versus separate regions — since the mouth needs to open, the jaw has to be its own joint under the head rather than fused geometry.

Working out the neck chain path and joint naming so it connects cleanly into the head joint, making sure the number of names matches the number of spans so there's no unwanted tip joint before the head begins.

Now I'm planning the head as a sweep following a forward-facing path from skull to muzzle, parented rigidly to the head joint, and sketching out the model-space coordinates for the skull back and muzzle front points.

Rather than a simple sweep, I'm considering using a loft for the head to get a more stylized blocky shape, defining stations from the back of the skull through the cheek and mid-face down to the muzzle, each with its own width and height values, and wondering whether the loft's cross-section defaults to a rounded rectangle or ellipse shape.

I want the head loft bound rigidly to the head bone, with a separate jaw loft hanging beneath the muzzle, jointed where the lower jaw meets the skull, tapering down to a small chin. For the coat, I'm leaning toward a pearly white with a faint lilac shimmer, blending between two near-white hex tones using noise so it doesn't look flat.
